Ibn Ashur y voit une réponse à cette objection et à celles qui en découlaient. Le verset se termine en affirmant que Dieu entend ce qu'on dit et voit ce qu'on fait, ce qui implique la rétribution. Les commentateurs ne se sont donc pas opposés sur le sens général, leurs divergences portant surtout sur les circonstances de la révélation et sur l'enchaînement avec les versets voisins.

Ce verset rappelle que Dieu fait pénétrer une partie de la nuit dans le jour et une partie du jour dans la nuit, si bien que l'un s'allonge tandis que l'autre raccourcit selon les saisons, et qu'il a assujetti le soleil et la lune, qui suivent chacun leur course jusqu'à un terme fixé. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Qatada entendent l'expression comme un gain et une perte alternés entre la nuit et le jour, tandis qu'al-Mawardi en donne plusieurs lectures, dont celle où l'été prend au terme de l'hiver et inversement, et celle où l'obscurité pénètre la lumière du jour et la lumière l'obscurité de la nuit. Presque tous s'accordent à identifier le terme fixé au Jour de la Résurrection. Qatada, Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Baydawi proposent toutefois que ce soit le moment où le soleil et la lune achèvent leur révolution, au terme de l'année pour le soleil et du mois pour la lune, comme l'indiquent al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Juzayy et Abu Hayyan. Al-Razi remarque que le verbe au présent pour la nuit et le jour marque un renouvellement quotidien, tandis que le passé pour le soleil et la lune marque une permanence, et il explique la mention première de la nuit par le fait que l'âme cherche davantage la cause de l'obscurité. Ibn Kathir rapporte en outre le hadith de Abu Dhar sur la prosternation du soleil sous le Trône, que les commentateurs ne reprennent pas tous. Les lectures de "ta'malun" à la deuxième personne ou à la troisième ne modifient pas le sens. Tous conviennent que le verset se conclut par l'affirmation que Dieu est parfaitement informé des actes des hommes, et que la création de ce cosmos atteste sa puissance et sa science.

Ce passage affirme que Dieu seul est la Vérité établie, que tout ce qui est adoré en dehors de Lui est vain et périssable, et qu'Il est le Très-Haut, le Grand, auquel toute créature est soumise. Les commentateurs rattachent le « cela » aux signes précédents : l'alternance de la nuit et du jour, l'assujettissement du soleil et de la lune, et les autres manifestations de la puissance divine, qui prouvent que Dieu est le Dieu véritable. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi y voient une preuve de l'unicité divine et de l'inanité de l'associationnisme. Al-Zamakhshari souligne que le pronom de séparation exprime l'exclusivité, tandis qu'al-Baydawi comprend le Vrai comme ce qui existe par soi et nécessairement. Sur le « vain », Mujahid l'identifie au démon, tandis que d'autres y voient les idoles et les statues ; Ibn Kathir et al-Tabari retiennent un sens plus large couvrant tout ce qui est adoré à la place de Dieu. Al-Mawardi explique que « le Très-Haut » désigne l'élévation de Son rang et « le Grand » celle de Son autorité, et al-Razi distingue les attributs de Sa perfection. Concernant la suite sur les navires et le passage de la tempête, les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que le verset est un rappel du bienfait divin. Ils divergent sur le « modéré » : al-Hasan y voit le croyant, Mujahid le mécréant qui cache son impiété, Ibn Abbas celui qui tient son engagement. Tous reconnaissent que le passage invite à la patience et à la reconnaissance envers Dieu.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset attire l'attention sur la navigation des bateaux sur la mer par la grâce de Dieu, et qu'il s'agit là d'un signe de Sa puissance et de Sa miséricorde. Al-Tabari en tire que ce mouvement prouve que Celui qui fait voguer les navires est la Vérité et que ce qu'on invoque en dehors de Lui est vain ; il ajoute que ces signes sont des leçons pour quiconque patiente face à ce qui est interdit par Dieu et remercie pour Ses bienfaits. Plusieurs savants, dont al-Baydawi et Ibn Juzayy, précisent que le mot « grâce » peut désigner la bienveillance de Dieu dans la mise en place des causes du voyage, le vent qui est lui-même un bienfait, ou encore les biens transportés par les navires. Tous s'accordent à dire que la patience et la gratitude sont les deux qualités du croyant, et que seul celui qui les réunit tire profit de ces signes ; al-Sha'bi rapporte que la patience est la moitié de la foi et la gratitude l'autre moitié. Dans le verset suivant, la majorité voit dans le « modéré » (muqtasid) un incroyant qui se tient dans un entre-deux, comme le dit Mujahid, tandis que al-Hasan y voit un croyant ferme dans le monothéisme et qu'Ibn Zayd le décrit comme celui qui reste mesuré dans sa conduite. Le terme « khattar » désigne presque unanimement le traître ; la trahison (khatr) est la pire des trahisons, et celui qui nie les signes de Dieu après avoir été sauvé a rompu son engagement envers son Seigneur.

Ce verset décrit l'attitude des gens en mer : lorsque des vagues les recouvrent comme des nuées ou des montagnes, ils invoquent Dieu seul en lui vouant leur religion ; une fois sauvés et arrivés à terre, ils se partagent en deux groupes. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et Ibn 'Atiyya rapportent que le « modéré » (muqtasid) désigne ici celui qui professe la foi de bouche tout en cachant l'incrédulité, selon Mujahid, tandis qu'al-Hasan, al-Naqqash et al-Baghawi y voient le croyant resté ferme dans le monothéisme et fidèle à son engagement pris en mer. Ibn Zayd et Ibn Kathir, dans un autre passage, entendent par là celui qui reste mesuré dans ses actes, et al-Zamakhshari estime que la sincérité née de la peur dure rarement chez quiconque. Tous s'accordent à dire que le khattar est le traître et que le khatr est la pire trahison ; la phrase finale fait du reniement des signes une conduite propre à celui qui réunit la trahison et l'ingratitude. Plusieurs récits, rapportés par al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi et al-Qurtubi, rattachent la révélation à 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl, qui, ayant fui en mer lors de la conquête de La Mecque, fut sauvé de la tempête puis embrassa l'islam. Le verset enseigne que Dieu met ses serviteurs à l'épreuve par l'adversité et la prospérité, et que le sabr et le shukr sont les qualités de celui qui tire profit des signes divins.

Le verset appelle tous les hommes à la crainte de Dieu et à la crainte d'un jour où aucun père ne pourra racheter son fils et aucun fils son père, car la promesse de Dieu est vraie. Que la vie d'ici-bas ne vous trompe donc pas, et que le Trompeur ne vous abuse pas au sujet de Dieu. La plupart des commentateurs entendent par « le Trompeur » le Diable, comme le disent Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada et Ibn Abbas, qui le décrit comme celui qui embellit les péchés et promet le pardon. Ibn Jurayj et d'autres y voient l'espérance vaine et le report de la repentance. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn Kathir ajoutent que l'ici-bas lui-même peut être une source de tromperie, et Sa'id ibn Jubayr rapporte qu'il s'agit de commettre le péché tout en espérant le pardon. Les exégètes s'accordent à voir dans ce jour le Jour de la Résurrection, où chacun ne se soucie que de soi, comme le dit Ibn Abbas. Certains rappellent que le discours peut viser en premier lieu les habitants de La Mecque, mais qu'il vaut pour tous. Sur le choix du mot « mawlud » plutôt que « walad », al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi et Abu al-Su'ud expliquent qu'il vise à couper l'espoir des croyants dont les pères étaient infidèles, tandis qu'Ibn 'Ashur y voit une nuance de filiation plus étroite. Les commentateurs rappellent aussi, à propos d'un autre passage de la sourate, que la connaissance de l'Heure et des cinq clés de l'invisible appartient à Dieu seul, selon le hadith authentique, et que nul ne sait quand viendra l'Heure, ce qu'est dans les matrices, ce que l'on gagnera demain ou en quelle terre on mourra. Tous s'accordent à inciter à hâter la repentance et les bonnes œuvres avant qu'il ne soit trop tard.

Ce verset affirme que Dieu seul connaît l'heure de la Résurrection, qu'Il fait descendre la pluie en son temps et en son lieu, qu'Il sait ce que contiennent les matrices, si l'enfant est mâle ou femelle, achevé ou non, heureux ou malheureux, et que nulle âme ne sait ce qu'elle gagnera demain ni en quelle terre elle mourra. Les exégètes s'accordent à voir dans ces cinq éléments les « clés de l'invisible » que Dieu seul possède, et s'appuient sur le hadith rapporté par Ibn 'Umar et d'autres. Ibn Mas'ud rapporte aussi que le Prophète n'a pas reçu la connaissance de ces cinq choses. La cause de révélation la plus répandue, transmise par Mujahid, concerne un homme du désert qui posa ces questions au Prophète. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir expliquent que la science réservée à Dieu est la connaissance complète et détaillée de ces réalités, tandis qu'Ibn Kathir et al-Razi rapportent aussi que Dieu peut en révéler une part à certains de ses serviteurs, comme les anges chargés des matrices. Al-Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi relèvent que le verbe « savoir » est attribué à Dieu et « connaître » à l'âme, car ce dernier implique la ruse et le calcul : l'homme, même en déployant tous ses moyens, ignore son gain et son lieu de mort. Ibn 'Atiyya et Abu Hayyan notent que ce que l'on déduit par l'expérience ou par des signes n'est pas ce savoir absolu. Al-Shawkani et al-Alusi soulignent que la fin du verset, qui qualifie Dieu d'Omniscient et de Parfaitement Informé, oppose la science totale de Dieu à l'ignorance des créatures.
en: The commentators generally agree that these disjointed letters at the opening of the surah have no clear meaning for most of them, and that the safest answer is that God alone knows what He intends by them. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi largely refer back to what was said at the beginning of al-Baqara. Some propose that they draw the listener's attention: al-Shawkani and al-Jaza'iri report that the polytheists forbade listening to the Quran, and that these unusual sounds compelled people to listen. Al-Sha'rawi sees in them a sign that the Quran is built from the very letters of the Arabic language, which makes its challenge stronger. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi note only that the surah is Meccan and that the exceptions are debated. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that the Book is described as wise, either in the sense of possessing wisdom or in the sense of being firmly established. The final point of agreement is that these letters belong to the divine mystery and cannot be explained literally.

The commentators explain that the phrase "these are the verses of the wise Book" refers to the verses of this surah and, more broadly, to the Qur'an. Al-Tabari reads it as verses that clarify and explain in detail. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings of "hakim": defined by lawful and unlawful rulings, perfectly sound, clearly from God, or showing wisdom by itself. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the word may mean possessing wisdom or describe God metaphorically. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the Book is guidance and mercy for the muhsinun. All agree that these are people who perform the prayer, pay zakat and firmly believe in the Hereafter. Al-Mawardi cites several explanations of ihsan, including the hadith of Gabriel defining it as worshipping God as though you see Him. Ibn Kathir says such people are upon guidance from their Lord and are the successful. On the reading of "wa rahmatan", Hamza reads it in the nominative, while al-Tabari, who accepts both readings, prefers the accusative. The occasion-of-revelation reports mostly concern the following verse about the one who buys frivolous talk. Ibn 'Uthaymin holds that the surah is Meccan in full unless a clear text says otherwise.

The commentators explain that the phrase guidance and mercy for the doers of good describes the Quran as a clear guide to the truth and a blessing for whoever acts upon it. The muhsinun, those who do good, are those who act well by following what God has revealed, and the verse itself identifies them as those who establish prayer, give zakat and are certain of the Hereafter. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir adopt this reading, and Ibn Kathir adds that this goodness covers voluntary acts and maintaining family ties. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan note that the word may also refer generally to all doers of good, the three named acts being singled out for their excellence. Ibn Atiyya, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan record differing views on the meaning of ihsan: for some it is faith, for al-Hasan it is prayer and kinship ties, and for Ibn Shajara it is the faith through which a person does good to himself. They cite the hadith of Gabriel defining ihsan as worshipping God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He sees you. The reading of Hamza with a nominative rahma is understood as a second predicate or as the predicate of an implied subject, while the accusative reading makes these words a circumstantial complement. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi report that the verses were revealed concerning the purchase of singing and idle entertainment, which Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan also accept. The commentators conclude that those who combine these qualities are upon guidance from their Lord and are the successful, meaning those who attain what they hope for and are spared what they fear.

This passage presents the Qur'an as guidance and mercy for the muhsinun, those who do good in their worship of God and in their dealings with others. They establish the prayer in its proper form, pay the obligatory zakat to its rightful recipients, and are certain of the Hereafter. The commentators explain that these three qualities are singled out for their excellence and illustrate ihsan without exhausting it. Al-Tabari holds that the muhsinun are those who act on what the Qur'an has revealed. He also records the variant reading: most readers take 'huda wa rahmatan' in the accusative as a circumstantial complement, while Hamza reads it in the nominative; al-Tabari prefers the accusative for its wide use.

Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan state that ihsan covers the highest good deeds, such as faith, prayer and charity, and that it refers to those who perceive the Qur'an as it truly is. Al-Razi links prayer to not imitating the Lord and zakat to meeting the needs of others. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi add that naming these three deeds is meant to highlight their value. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di describe prayer as the foundation of sincerity and communion with God, and zakat as a purification of the soul from miserliness.

The commentators agree that the muhsinun are upon guidance from their Lord and are the successful ones. They define success as attaining what is sought and escaping what is feared, in this world and the next. Ibn 'Ashur notes that in the early period zakat was left to the generosity of believers, with no fixed amount or time.

The commentators explain that this verse concludes the description of the good-doers who establish prayer, give zakat and firmly believe in the Hereafter. These people are upon guidance from their Lord, meaning a clear path and a light, and they are the successful ones who attain what they hope for and escape what they flee, in this world and the next. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand this guidance as a clear method and manifest insight granted by God to whoever follows the Book, while Ibn Sallam takes it to mean the clarification itself. As for the word "the successful", Ibn 'Abbas says they are those who obtained what they sought and were saved from what they fled, Ibn Sallam and Qatada take them to be the blessed, Ibn Shajara the ones who prosper, and al-Naqqash the winners, all fairly close in meaning. The scholars agree that this guidance is a gift from God that sustains the believer on the path of truth, and that success results from soundness of belief together with righteous action. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the verse follows the description of the Book as wise, guiding and merciful, in order to show the fruit of following it. The commentators do not differ on the general meaning of the verse, their disagreements concern particular wording, and none of them settles the question in favour of one view.

This verse describes a type of person who prefers idle talk that distracts from the good to the words of God, in order to lead people astray from God's way without knowledge, and who mock God's path or His signs. The verse threatens them with a humiliating punishment. The commentators agree on the general meaning: idle talk refers to any speech that diverts from remembering God and from what is good. They differ on its precise identification. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrima, Mujahid and al-Hasan take it to mean singing, and al-Qurtubi calls this the highest view stated. Al-Tabari, who prefers a broader reading, holds that it covers singing and other speech of the same kind, a view Ibn Kathir also adopts. Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd take it to mean polytheism, while Qatada takes it to mean all play and frivolity. Several reports link the verse to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who bought stories of Persian kings to tell the Quraysh and turn them from the Qur'an, and others to a man who bought singing slave-girls. On recitation, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Ya'qub read "wa yattakhidha" in the accusative, coordinated with "li-yudilla", while the rest read it in the nominative, coordinated with "yashtari". Al-Tabari regards both readings as close in meaning. The exegetes explain that leading astray means turning people from God's religion and from reciting the Qur'an, and that "without knowledge" means ignorance of the outcome.

This verse describes the person who, when the verses of God are recited to him, turns away arrogantly as though he had not heard them, as though there were a heaviness in his ears. The Prophet is then told to give him the tidings of a painful punishment, the tidings being used here ironically. The commentators agree on the plain sense: refusing to listen to the Quran out of pride, and the comparison with one who does not hear, or who is deaf, means that he gains nothing from what he hears, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy explain. Al-Razi stresses that arrogance is graver than mere turning away. The preceding verse is where the scholars differ most. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take 'idle talk' to mean singing, al-Dahhak takes it to mean polytheism, 'Ata' to mean falsehood, and al-Hasan to mean anything that distracts from the remembrance of God. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi report that it was revealed about al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who told the Quraysh tales of the Persian kings to draw them away from the Quran, while Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir include singing within its meaning. All agree that the refusal to hear the truth after hearing it comes from pride. These views are reported as they stand, and the commentators do not judge between them.

This passage announces the reward of those who believe and do righteous deeds: they will have the Gardens of Bliss, where they will remain forever. The commentators explain that this is a promise from God, true and without fail, and that God is the Mighty, who cannot be overcome, and the Wise in His acts and His promises. According to al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi, the phrases “promise of God” and “truly” are two emphatic expressions: the first stresses the promise itself, the second stresses the promise expressed in the previous phrase. Ibn Kathir describes these gardens as offering every kind of pleasure, including food, drink, dwellings, mounts, spouses and delights no one has imagined. Al-Alusi notes that attaching “gardens” to “bliss” signals that the bliss is abundant and well known, and he quotes a saying attributed to Malik ibn Dinar about the location of these gardens, without vouching for its authenticity. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani understand the “righteous deeds” as the practical expression of faith, and the gardens as the counterpart to the believers' response to the verses. Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi stress the link between faith and action, since faith must show itself in conduct. Al-Razi points to several subtleties of wording, including the single punishment set against plural gardens, which he takes to show that mercy outweighs wrath. The commentators agree that the verse brings good news to believers, in contrast with the fate of those who turn arrogantly away from the verses.

This part of the verse states that those who believe and do righteous deeds will abide forever in the Gardens of Bliss, and that this is a true promise from God. It ends by describing God as the Mighty, whom nothing can overcome or prevent from fulfilling His promise or threat, and the Wise, who acts only as wisdom and benefit require. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan, read it as the counterpart to the fate of those who turn away from the Quran, described just before. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the two phrases "abiding forever" and "a true promise" are grammatical emphases: the first reinforces the meaning of the promise itself, the second confirms the whole statement as a promise. Abu Hayyan notes that a reading attributed to Zayd ibn Ali makes "abiding" a second predicate. Al-Razi points to several stylistic subtleties: God's mercy in reward is wider than His anger in punishment, and the good news is presented as coming from God Himself, which underlines its greatness. Ibn Kathir specifies that the people of Paradise enjoy every kind of pleasure, food, dwelling, mount and companion, and never seek to leave. On the two divine names, the commentators broadly agree: the Mighty is the one whom nothing overcomes, and the Wise is the one who orders all things rightly.

This verse describes the greatness of God's creation: He raised the heavens without pillars that you can see, placed firm mountains in the earth so that it would not sway with its people, spread every kind of creature across it, and sent down water from the sky by which He made grow every noble kind of plant. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'without pillars you can see'. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and Mujahid say the heavens have pillars that are unseen, while al-Hasan and Qatada say they have no pillars at all; al-Razi concludes that their staying up is by God's power, and al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi note that the clause may be a separate statement. On 'lest it sway with you', most read it as 'lest it sway', while Yahya ibn Sallam and al-Naqqash explain it as 'lest it move' or 'lest it shift away'. al-Mawardi reports that the earth once tilted like a ship until God anchored it with mountains. All agree that 'creatures' means anything that moves on the earth. For 'every noble kind', Ibn Abbas and Qatada take it as beautiful, al-Sha'bi takes it to refer to people who are noble or base depending on whether they enter Paradise or Hell, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya understand 'pair' as 'kind'. The commentators link the verse to the rebuke of those who buy frivolous talk, and read it as proof of the Creator's oneness against the idolaters, who cannot show anything their gods have created. The verse concludes that the wrongdoers are in clear error.

This passage states that everything just mentioned, the heavens, the earth, the mountains, the animals, the rain and the plants, is the creation of God alone, and it challenges the polytheists to show what their deities have created apart from Him. They cannot. Most commentators take the word creation to mean the created things that have been listed, and the question as a rebuke and a challenge meant to silence them. Al-Tabari, Qatada, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur identify those 'other than Him' as the idols. Al-Sa'di and al-Shinqiti draw from the acknowledgement of divine creation the obligation to worship Him alone. For al-Tabari, the 'clear error' is an error that becomes plain to anyone who reflects with his mind. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read the closing phrase as a shift from rebuke to recording their error against them. Abu Hayyan notes that using the explicit noun instead of a pronoun shows that they have placed polytheism where it does not belong. On the heavens without pillars, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi give two readings: either there are unseen pillars, or there are none at all. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the second the sounder and the majority view. Ibn 'Uthaymin argues that this verse does not establish that the earth rotates, and he regards such an inference as open to question, the Qur'anic text being the reference. Ibn al-Qayyim observes that the challenge to see is more forceful than a mere statement.

This verse states that God gave Luqman wisdom, which the commentators define as understanding of the religion, sound reason and rightness in speech and action, and that the first thing he was bidden to do was to give thanks to God. The exegetes explain that gratitude benefits the grateful person himself, since it preserves the blessing and draws more of it, while God is self-sufficient and worthy of praise whether people thank Him or reject Him. Most scholars, including al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir, hold that Luqman was a wise righteous man rather than a prophet, whereas Ikrima and al-Sha'bi said he was a prophet, a view Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya consider weak because of its chain of transmission. Opinions also differ on his origin and trade: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab describe him as a black slave, while others say he was a carpenter, a tailor or a shepherd. On the particle in "an ushkur", al-Zamakhshari and al-Nahhas take it as explanatory, since giving wisdom amounts to a saying, while al-Zajjaj takes it as meaning "so that". Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur note that gratitude belongs to wisdom because it puts the most important thing first. Ibn Ashur also observes that many sayings attributed to Luqman are not authenticated, so the Quran's own account is the firm basis here.

This verse reports that Luqman, while advising his son, forbade him to associate anything with God, explaining that association is a tremendous wrong, meaning the placing of worship where it does not belong. The commentators agree that this counsel is the core of the wisdom God gave Luqman, and that forbidding polytheism is the first thing an exhortation should address. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya take the wrong to be association itself, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that it is a wrong because it equates one who has no blessing except from God with one who has no blessing from Him at all. A report in the two Sahihs states that the Prophet ﷺ explained that the word wrong in the verse about those who believed without mixing their faith with wrongdoing refers to association; Ibn al-Qayyim adds that the absolute wrong that removes security and guidance is polytheism. Scholars differ on whether Luqman was a prophet. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, hold that he was a wise man and not a prophet, while Ikrima, al-Sha'bi and al-Suddi say he was a prophet. Some report that Luqman's son was an associator whom his father kept advising until he embraced faith, though others note that a prohibition can be issued out of fear that something may happen. The son's name is given variously as Anam, Mishkam or Tharan. Most exegetes also link the following verses on parents to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his mother.

This verse states that God enjoined humanity to be good to its parents, for the mother bore the child in weakness upon weakness and nursed him until weaning within two years, and he is commanded to be thankful to God and to his parents, since the return is to God alone. The commentators agree that the verse stresses the rights of parents, particularly the mother, because of the hardships of pregnancy, childbirth and nursing. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Dahhak explain wahn as hardship, toil and weakness, while Mujahid reports that it refers to the weakness of the child upon the weakness of the mother. As for gratitude, Sufyan ibn Uyayna holds that whoever prays the five daily prayers has thanked God, and whoever prays for his parents after them has thanked his parents. On the length of nursing, al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad and Ahmad hold it to be two years, whereas Abu Hanifa holds thirty months, relying on the verse of al-Ahqaf. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi see the passage as a parenthetical insertion within Luqman's advice to his son, and Ibn 'Atiyya argues that the mother has three degrees of claim to honour against one for the father, based on the well-known hadith. Several exegetes report that the verse was revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his mother, though Ibn 'Ashur finds this context ill-suited. The commentators also note that obedience to parents does not extend to associating others with God, that one should keep them company kindly, and that one should follow the path of those who turn to God.

The commentators explain that the verse tells the believer to treat his parents kindly and to keep their company properly in this world, but that if they strive to make him associate others with God, of which he has no knowledge, he must not obey them in that. It sits within Luqman's counsel to his son against polytheism, and several scholars, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, treat it as an interjection that reinforces that advice. All agree that associating partners with God is a great wrong, and that parents are not obeyed in disobedience to God, while the believer still keeps good company with them.

Opinions differ on the occasion of revelation. Most, including al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, report that it was sent down concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, whose mother swore she would neither eat nor drink until he abandoned his faith. Others, such as Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi, hold that the verse is general. Ibn 'Abbas, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Sam'ani, took "the one who turns back to God" to mean Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, while others understood it to mean the Prophet or the believers in general.

On the duration of nursing, the majority accept two years, and Ibn Kathir draws from this the minimum length of pregnancy as six months. Abu Hanifa, according to al-Zamakhshari, takes thirty months. The commentators also note that the mother is due greater kindness, since the Prophet repeated "your mother" three times before saying "your father".

This verse records Luqman's advice to his son: God knows every deed, good or bad, however small, even the weight of a mustard seed, whether hidden in a rock, in the heavens or in the earth, and He will bring it forth to account on the Day of Judgment. The commentators agree that God is subtle in extracting it and aware of its exact place, and that the verse warns against belittling any good or evil act. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take the pronoun 'innaha' to refer to the wrongdoing or the deed, whereas some grammarians see it as the pronoun of the matter; al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi discuss the reading with 'mithqal' in the nominative. As for the rock, Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi describe a rock beneath the seven earths, which al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya consider weakly supported, while Qatada takes it to mean a mountain. Ibn Kathir explains 'yati bi-ha Allah' as bringing it forth to be judged, and al-Tabari notes that some take it to mean that God knows it. Al-Razi reads the sequence of places as a progression of concealment: smallness, enclosure, distance and darkness.

The commentators explain this verse as Luqman's advice to his son: to establish the prayer with its proper conditions, to enjoin good and forbid evil, and to bear patiently what befalls him, for these are matters that require resolve. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the patience mainly as enduring harm suffered while commanding right and forbidding wrong, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it as a general patience in every trial. All agree that prayer and reforming others are central. As for the phrase ʿazm al-umur, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya give several readings: matters Allah has enjoined, or noble qualities adopted by people of sound judgment. Al-Tabari prefers the first, and Ibn Atiyya judges it the more correct. Al-Razi notes that one who exhorts must first perfect himself. Ibn Kathir, citing many hadiths, links the passage to the prohibitions that follow on pride, arrogant gait and raised voice. Al-Qurtubi notes that Ibn Abbas considered patience to be part of true faith. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir also observe that the duty to do good falls on each person according to his capacity, not on the father alone.

This verse forbids arrogance both in dealing with people and in one's gait. Most commentators explain "do not turn your cheek away from people" as turning one's face from others in contempt and haughtiness, as Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak say. The word sa'r originally denotes a camel's disease that twists its neck, and this was used as an image of the proud person. Mujahid takes it to mean shunning someone with whom one has a grudge, while Ibrahim al-Nakha'i takes it as affectation in speech. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas adds that the poor and the rich should be treated alike. "Do not walk on the earth exultantly" means, for most, not walking with conceit and swagger; al-Zamakhshari notes that the blameworthy walk is that which comes from idleness and wantonness rather than need. The mukhtal is one who regards himself as superior, and the fakhur is one who counts his blessings without thanking God, or who boasts over others, as reported from Mujahid and Ibn Shajara. The commentators agree that God does not love the arrogant and boastful, and that the verse gives the reason for the prohibition. Several observe that the image of the diseased camel and the braying donkey carries a clear sense of blame, the donkey being a byword for baseness among the Arabs. These counsels are presented as the words of Luqman to his son, and the verse completes what precedes it on prayer and enjoining good.

This verse records Luqman's counsel to his son: walk with moderation and lower your voice. The commentators explain that moderation in walking means, for Mujahid, humility, for Qatada, the avoidance of arrogance, and for Yazid ibn Abi Habib, the avoidance of haste. Al-Tabari concludes that the meaning includes both humility and not hurrying. Regarding the voice, most understand that it should be restrained and raised only when needed. The comparison with the donkey's bray is read by al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi as a strong expression of blame: the most hideous of voices is that of the donkey, whose braying begins with a rasping breath and ends with a sigh. Al-Zamakhshari sees a powerful metaphor meant to discourage shouting, and Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di draw the same lesson of avoiding needless raised voices. Some report an opinion attributed to Sufyan al-Thawri that everything glorifies God except the donkey, but the majority do not adopt it. Al-Razi offers several reasons for singling out the donkey, including its proverbial status among the Arabs, who also prided themselves on loud voices. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the word ankar signifies what is repugnant, and that the plural form of the donkeys is chosen for rhyme.

This passage of Surah Luqman recalls that God subjected to humankind what is in the heavens and on the earth, the sun, the moon, the stars, the clouds, the rivers, the trees, the animals and the minerals, so that they may benefit from them, and that He completed His favours upon them, both outward and inward. The commentators differ on their meaning. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid take the outward favour to be Islam, good character and victory, and the inward one to be the concealment of sins, while al-Dahhak understands fine appearance and balanced limbs, with the inward favour being knowledge. Al-Muhasibi distinguishes the blessings of this world from those of the hereafter, and others hold that the outward is what is perceived by the senses and the inward what is known only through reasoning. Nearly all agree that these favours include both worldly life and religion, and that the wording of the verse embraces all these views. The readings differ between the singular "ni'mah", understood as a collective noun denoting abundance, and the plural "ni'amahu"; some report that the singular refers to the testimony of faith. The verse then censures those who dispute about God without knowledge, guidance or an illuminating book. The exegetes identify them with the Meccans, such as al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, though some say a Jew who questioned the Prophet about his Lord. They agree that this is vain argument grounded in blind imitation: when they are called to follow what God has sent down, they reply that they will follow what their fathers followed, and the verse answers that they should not follow them even if Satan were calling their fathers to the torment of the blazing fire. The commentators conclude that the subject is blameworthy controversy and that blind imitation cannot serve as proof.

This verse reports the answer of the polytheists when they are told to follow what Allah has sent down: they say they will follow instead what they found their fathers doing. God replies with a rhetorical question of reproach: would they follow them even if Satan were calling their fathers to the torment of the Blazing Fire? The general meaning, shared by most commentators, is that blind imitation of forebears cannot count as proof, since it is Satan who makes falsehood attractive. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that these fathers followed a misguidance that Satan had made appealing to them. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy hold that the question implies a negative answer, and that the verb is understood as: they should not follow them. Al-Razi notes that a revealed word is clearer than the deeds of the ignorant, so the word of God must be preferred. Al-Baydawi and al-Alusi read the verse as prohibiting imitation in matters of belief, while noting that scholars disagree about other matters. Ibn Sa'di stresses that Satan feels no affection for these ancestors but is hostile to them. Regarding the blessings mentioned in the previous verse, the commentators differ: Ibn Abbas takes the outward blessing to be Islam and good form, and the hidden one to be the sins God conceals; Mujahid links them to the spread of Islam and the help of the angels; al-Dahhak to beauty of form and knowledge. Al-Qurtubi notes that the verse was linked by some transmissions to a Jew or to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. The overall message remains a condemnation of blind imitation and of disputing without knowledge.

This verse in Surah Luqman says that whoever submits his face to Allah, meaning he devotes his worship and heart sincerely to Him while doing good in his deeds, has grasped the most secure handhold. The commentators agree that "the firmest handhold" is an image for something that does not break and cannot be feared to break, and that "the outcome of all affairs" returns to Allah alone, who will reward each person accordingly.

They differ somewhat on what "submitting" means. Al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas understand it as sincerity toward Allah, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir as entrusting one's affair to Him, and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya as confident reliance and surrender. Ibn Kathir takes "doing good" to mean following the revealed law in one's actions. As for "the firmest handhold," Ibn Abbas identifies it with the declaration that there is no god but Allah, Anas with the Quran, al-Suddi with Islam, and Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd with loving and hating for the sake of Allah. Al-Mawardi offers two reasons for the image: the one who holds it secures himself, and it resembles a firm structure that does not come apart.

The commentators link the verse to the condemnation of those who blindly follow their fathers. Ibn Kathir sees the verses that follow as a consolation to the Prophet regarding the disbelief of some people. Al-Qurtubi notes that worship without good conduct and knowledge of the heart is of no benefit. Ibn Juzayy and others simply refer to parallel verses without further elaboration.

This verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ about those who reject faith: their disbelief should not grieve him, because they will return to God, who will inform them of their deeds and repay them, for He knows what the breasts conceal. The commentators agree on the general sense: do not be saddened by the refusal of the disbelievers, since the outcome belongs to God. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that God gives them a brief enjoyment in this life and then compels them toward a harsh punishment, the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari sees in the word 'compel' an image of an unavoidable constraint, and Ibn 'Atiyya reads it as a metaphor for the grip of punishment. Al-Qurtubi notes that 'man' can refer to one or many, which explains the alternation between singular and plural pronouns. Al-Razi offers a subtle reading: the shame of having denied the prophets leads the disbelievers to prefer the Fire to standing before their Lord in the presence of the prophets. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the verb means 'to worry', and Abu al-Su'ud and al-Zamakhshari note that the reading 'yuhzinuka' is less common. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the prohibition of grief is attributed to the disbelief as a figurative device. Ibn al-Jawzi rejects the claim that this verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword, since consolation does not contradict the command to fight. Ibn Sa'di argues that if there were any good in these people, God would have guided them. Most commentators understand 'dhat al-sudur' as what hearts conceal of disbelief and preference for Satan.

This verse states that God grants the disbelievers a brief period of enjoyment of this world's goods, after which He will compel them towards a severe punishment. The commentators explain that "We let them enjoy" means granting them respite and prolonging their lives, and that "We compel them" means forcing them and driving them. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi identify the "severe punishment" as the punishment of Hell. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the adjective "thick" or "harsh" is borrowed from heavy physical bodies and conveys the severity and weight of the torment on the one who suffers it. There is broad agreement that worldly enjoyment is very small compared with the eternal bliss of the Hereafter. The verse also consoles the Prophet, whose grief at his people's disbelief is eased: their return is to God, who knows what hearts conceal. Al-Razi notes that one who expects his truth to prevail does not grieve, whereas one who has no such hope suffers. On the idea of compulsion, al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi cite a tradition in which the burning inhabitants of Hell ask for cold, and are sent the zamharir, so that they then desire the flames again out of compulsion. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the sentence is an explanatory aside answering the question of why the punishment is delayed.

This verse reports that if the polytheists are asked who created the heavens and the earth, they answer that it is Allah. The Prophet is then told to say, "Praise be to Allah," which the commentators read as a conclusion that binds them to their own admission, and the verse adds that most of them do not know what this entails. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud take the praise as an obligation placed on them: since the Creator alone deserves praise and worship, nothing may be associated with Him, and Abu al-Su'ud adds that the proofs of Divine oneness are so clear that even the obstinate can hardly deny them. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi stress that the pagans acknowledge Allah as sole Creator yet worship others whom they regard as His creatures and property. Al-Razi links the verse to the preceding passage: it consoles the Prophet, since the truth of his message will become evident when people return to Allah. He offers two readings of "they do not know": either they do not know that all praise belongs to Allah, or they have no knowledge at all that would restrain them from denying the truth. All agree that whatever is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, that He has no need of His creatures, and that He is worthy of praise. Al-Tabari notes that this ownership includes even idols, and Ibn 'Ashur observes that the verse continues the criticism of blindly following ancestors.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms that everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, as creation, possession and servitude, so that He alone deserves to be worshipped. It also states that God is rich, independent of His creatures, and worthy of praise. The verse comes after the polytheists have acknowledged that God created the heavens and the earth, and it draws the logical conclusion that all sovereignty belongs to God, including the idols and other objects of worship. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi largely agree on this sense: God's wealth means that He has no need of the worlds, their praise or their worship, and the Praiseworthy is the one who deserves praise even if no one praises Him. Al-Razi understands richness as freedom from need despite the abundance of what God possesses, and the Praiseworthy as the one praised in every respect. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the pronoun 'huwa' expresses that wealth and praise belong to God exclusively, and that the verse denies the gods of the polytheists any wealth or claim to praise. On the central meaning the commentators do not diverge; they vary only in how they define praise. Ibn 'Uthaymin takes it as praise due for God's act of creation and His legislation, while others see it as an intrinsic worthiness. Al-Qurtubi links the praise to God's guidance toward the religion. No commentary here draws a legal ruling or a specific occasion of revelation; the exegetes connect the verse to what precedes it, the polytheists' acknowledgement, and to what follows, the words of God.

This verse teaches that the words of God never run out. Even if every tree on earth became a pen and the sea, extended by seven more seas, became ink, the pens would break and the ink would run dry before God's words were exhausted. Commentators agree that the number seven signifies abundance rather than a fixed limit. Al-Tabari, al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatada report that the verse answers the unbelievers, who claimed the Quran would soon come to an end, or the Jews, who boasted that the Torah contained everything. Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and others relate, through Ibn 'Abbas, that it was revealed in reply to the rabbis who asked the Prophet how he could say that little knowledge had been given to people when they possessed the Torah. Ibn 'Atiyya regards this as the sound account and considers the verse Medinan, whereas others hold it to be Meccan. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi understand the words as God's eternal speech or as the things He decrees, and al-Qushayri prefers the first meaning. Ibn Kathir, quoting al-Rabi' ibn Anas, adds that human knowledge is like a drop beside God's knowledge. The statement that your creation and resurrection are no more difficult than that of a single soul means that for God creating and raising all of humanity is as easy as doing so for one person. The verse ends by affirming that God is mighty and wise.

The commentators explain that the creation of all of you and your resurrection are, for God, no harder than the creation and resurrection of a single soul, since when He wills a thing He says to it "Be," and it is. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take from this that for God the few and the many are equal. Ibn Kathir stresses that this power is complete and that God does not need to repeat His command. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read in it an image of God's knowledge: He hears every sound and sees every thing in a single instant, without attending to one thing preventing Him from attending to another, and the same applies to creation and resurrection. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi report that the verse was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf and his companions, who found it hard to believe that a human formed in stages could be raised all at once. Ibn Ashur sees the verse as a reply to this objection and to the doubts that arose from it. It ends by affirming that God hears what is said and sees what is done, which implies the requital of deeds. The commentators therefore do not disagree on the general meaning. Their differences concern mainly the circumstances of revelation and how the verse connects with the verses around it.

This verse describes how God makes part of the night enter the day and part of the day enter the night, so that one lengthens while the other shortens with the seasons, and how He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running its course toward a appointed term. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Qatada understand this as the alternating gain and loss between night and day, while al-Mawardi offers several readings, including that summer takes from winter and winter from summer, and that darkness enters the light of day and light enters the darkness of night. Nearly all agree that the appointed term is the Day of Resurrection. Qatada, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi, however, take it to mean the moment when the sun and moon complete their revolution, at the end of the year for the sun and the month for the moon, a view also given by al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan. Al-Razi observes that the present tense for night and day signals daily renewal, while the past tense for the sun and moon signals continuity, and he explains why night is mentioned first by saying the soul seeks the cause of darkness more than the cause of light. Ibn Kathir also cites the hadith of Abu Dhar about the sun prostrating beneath the Throne, a report not every commentator accepts. The variant readings of "ta'maluna" as second or third person do not change the meaning. All agree the verse closes by affirming that God is fully aware of what people do, and that the order of this cosmos demonstrates His power and knowledge.

This passage states that God alone is the established Truth, that whatever is worshipped besides Him is vain and passing, and that He is the Most High, the Great, to whom all creation is subject. The commentators link the word 'that' to the signs just mentioned: the alternation of night and day, the subjection of the sun and moon, and other displays of divine power, which prove that God is the true God. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take this as evidence of God's oneness and the falsehood of associating partners with Him. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the separating pronoun expresses exclusivity, while al-Baydawi understands the Truth as what exists necessarily and in itself. On the word 'vain', Mujahid takes it to mean Satan, while others mean the idols; Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari prefer a broader sense covering anything worshipped instead of God. Al-Mawardi explains 'the Most High' as elevated in rank and 'the Great' as supreme in authority. The following verses about ships and the storm are read by the commentators as a reminder of God's favour. They differ on the 'moderate' one: al-Hasan says he is a believer, Mujahid says a disbeliever who hides his unbelief, and Ibn Abbas says one who keeps his covenant. All agree the passage calls for patience and gratitude.

The commentators explain that the verse draws attention to ships sailing on the sea by God's favour, and that this is one of His signs showing His power and mercy. Al-Tabari takes from it that this motion proves that the One who causes the ships to run is the Truth, and that what is invoked besides Him is false; he adds that these signs are lessons for everyone who is patient in refraining from what God forbids and grateful for His blessings. Several scholars, including al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy, note that the word 'favour' may refer to God's kindness in providing the means of the voyage, to the wind itself as a blessing, or to the goods the ships carry. There is broad agreement that patience and gratitude are the two qualities of the believer and that only one who combines them benefits from these signs; al-Sha'bi reports that patience is half of faith and gratitude the other half. In the next verse, most read the 'moderate' (muqtasid) as an unbeliever who stays in between, as Mujahid says, while al-Hasan takes it to mean a believer firm in monotheism and Ibn Zayd understands it as one who keeps a balanced course in his deeds. The word 'khattar' is almost unanimously explained as treacherous; treachery (khatr) is the worst form of betrayal, and whoever denies God's signs after being saved has broken his covenant with his Lord.

This verse describes how people behave at sea: when waves cover them like canopies or mountains, they call upon God alone, devoting their religion to Him, but once He brings them safely to land they divide into two groups. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report that the muqtasid here is the one who professes faith with his tongue while concealing disbelief, as Mujahid said, whereas al-Hasan, al-Naqqash and al-Baghawi take him to be the believer who stayed firm in monotheism and kept the covenant made at sea. Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir, in another passage, understand the moderate as one who is balanced in his deeds, and al-Zamakhshari notes that the sincerity born of fear rarely lasts in anyone. The commentators agree that the khattar is the treacherous one and that khatr is the worst kind of betrayal; the closing phrase makes denying the signs the conduct of one who combines treachery and ingratitude. Several reports, cited by al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, link the revelation to 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl, who fled by sea at the conquest of Mecca, was saved from a storm, and then embraced Islam. The verse teaches that God tests His servants through hardship and ease, and that patience and gratitude are the qualities of one who benefits from God's signs.

The verse calls all people to be mindful of their Lord and to fear a day when no parent will avail his child and no child will avail his parent, because God's promise is true. Let the life of this world not deceive you, nor the Deceiver deceive you about God. Most commentators identify the Deceiver as Satan, following Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada and Ibn Abbas, who describe him as the one who adorns sins and promises forgiveness. Ibn Jurayj and others take it to mean false hope and the postponement of repentance. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir add that this world itself can be a deception, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr explains it as committing sin while expecting forgiveness. The exegetes agree that the day is the Day of Resurrection, when each person is concerned only with himself, as Ibn Abbas says. Some note that the address may first be aimed at the people of Mecca, but its meaning extends to all. On why the verse says mawlud rather than walad, al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that this closes the hope of believers whose fathers died in disbelief that they might benefit them in the Hereafter, while Ibn 'Ashur sees a finer nuance of close filiation. Elsewhere in the surah, commentators note that knowledge of the Hour and the five keys of the unseen belongs to God alone, as the authentic hadith states: no one knows when the Hour will come, what the wombs hold, what one will earn tomorrow, or in which land one will die. All agree that the verse urges hastening repentance and good deeds before it is too late.

This verse states that God alone knows when the Hour will come, that He sends down rain at the time and place He determines, and that He knows what wombs contain, whether a child is male or female, complete or incomplete, and whether it will be fortunate or wretched. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, nor in which land it will die. The commentators agree that these five matters are the keys of the unseen that God has kept to Himself, and they cite the authentic hadith transmitted through Ibn Umar and others. Ibn Mas'ud also reports that the Prophet was not given knowledge of these five. The most widely transmitted occasion of revelation, related by Mujahid, concerns a Bedouin man who asked the Prophet these questions. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the knowledge reserved to God is the complete, detailed knowledge of these realities, while Ibn Kathir and al-Razi also note that God may reveal part of it to some servants, such as the angels assigned to the wombs. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi observe that knowing is ascribed to God and mere awareness to the soul, because the latter carries the sense of scheming and calculation: a person, however much he strives, does not know his gain or his place of death. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that what people learn through experience or signs is not this absolute knowledge. Al-Shawkani and al-Alusi stress that the verse closes by describing God as All-Knowing and All-Aware, contrasting His complete knowledge with the ignorance of creatures.
